title: Where, When, and How Many Bits? Scaling Laws for SGD with Stochastic Rounding

paper.title: Where, When, and How Many Bits? Scaling Laws for SGD with Stochastic Rounding
paper.abstract:
Abstract Low-precision training reduces computation but introduces additional rounding error.
We study how stochastic rounding (SR) affects prediction risk as model size,
training time and precision change. We consider a two-layer linear network
with a fixed random first layer, trained by mini-batch SGD on fresh Gaussian
data with power-law spectra. At each SGD step, the features used in forward and backward
computations are rounded independently. We prove matched upper and lower
bounds on prediction error for the final model and for uniform parameter
averaging, with general learning-rate and precision schedules chosen before training.
For fixed precisions and constant learning rates with parameter averaging,
we derive how the smallest prediction error decreases with compute and
identify model sizes and training times that achieve this optimal-compute scaling. Rounding only the forward features preserves the compute
scaling of exact arithmetic, while rounding backward features changes it.
Averaging parameters can change which computation needs higher
precision and when higher precision is useful. The laws also give bit
requirements for a given accuracy tolerance and show how backward rounding changes
learning-rate schedule design. At a fixed compute budget, lower precision can improve prediction when the benefit of a larger model or longer training outweighs
the additional SR-induced error. Model simulations illustrate these tradeoffs,
and experiments with an MLP and a small transformer examine rounding choices
beyond the theoretical model.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Training large machine learning models in low precision can reduce memory usage and computational costs. For example, mixed-precision training computes matrix multiplications of the forward and backward passes in 16-bit arithmetic while keeping a high-precision copy of the weights ( Micikevicius et al., 2018 ) . Recent LLMs are even pretrained with 8-bit and 4-bit floating-point matrix products ( Micikevicius et al., 2022 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2024 ; Tseng et al., 2025 ; Castro et al., 2025 ; Chmiel et al., 2025 ; Panferov et al., 2026 ) . Meanwhile, quantization-aware training (QAT) simulates low-precision weights and activations during training, making the trained model run in low precision at inference ( Jacob et al., 2018 ; Esser et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . A third setting saves training memory by quantizing the activations saved for backpropagation, while leaving the forward pass unchanged ( Chen et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) . Separately, Chen et al. (2020) show extra gradient variance caused by rounding in fully quantized training, where weights, activations and gradients are quantized. In this paper, we focus on the first setting, in which the arithmetic of training itself is rounded. Stochastic rounding (SR) rounds a number to one of its neighboring representable values with probabilities that preserve the input value in expectation. This unbiasedness can avoid update stagnation at precisions where round-to-nearest stalls ( Gupta et al., 2015 ; Zhang et al., 2017 ; De Sa et al., 2018 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Ozkara et al., 2025 ) . Existing SR theory provides probabilistic bounds on rounding errors in numerical computations ( Higham and Mary, 2019 ; Higham and Mary, 2020 ; Connolly et al., 2021 ; Croci et al., 2022 ; El Arar et al., 2023 ; Drineas and Ipsen, 2024 ; El Arar et al., 2026 ) and convergence guarantees for low-precision SGD ( Li et al., 2017 ; De Sa et al., 2018 ; Ozkara et al., 2025 ) . Its benefit on small singular values has also been studied ( Boutsikas et al., 2024 ; Dexter et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . These results do not further describe how prediction risk depends jointly on model width, training time and precision, or how to allocate precision bits across operations and training steps. So we aim to answer the following question in this paper: Where, when, and with how many bits should we use stochastic rounding during training? To answer this question, we prove a neural scaling law, which describes how loss asymptotically decreases with model size, training time and compute ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ; Subramanian et al., 2026 ) , This law practically guides the allocation of compute resources during training. Recent empirical work extends these laws to low-precision training and model quantization ( Kumar et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Frantar et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . Typically, Kumar et al. (2025) ; Sun et al. (2025) empirically use fitted scaling laws to choose model size, training data and precision for a given compute budget. These findings motivate a theoretical study of precision-dependent loss scaling and quantitative analyses of training dynamics with quantization ( Zhang et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . In the exact-arithmetic setting, theory of neural scaling law has been extensively studied ( Bahri et al., 2024 ; Maloney et al., 2022 ; Bordelon et al., 2024 ; Paquette et al., 2024 ; Paquette et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2025 ; Bordelon and Mori, 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) . Specifically, Paquette et al. (2024) gives the baseline compute optimal scaling law. We follow these results and study a two-layer linear network with a fixed random first layer and train its output layer using online SGD with SR. We consider both the final model and a model formed by averaging parameters during training. And the features used in the forward and backward computations are rounded independently, possibly at different precisions over the training. Kim et al. (2026) concurrently fit separate forward/backward precision effects and hardware-aware allocations, supported by a convex-optimization upper bound. We theoretically derive binary-SR risk scaling laws and optimal compute allocations in low precision. Figure 1: (a) We round the features either at forward pass or backward pass in SGD dynamics ( 5 ) with one-bit precision and compare the SR-induced error over the corresponding risk without rounding. Solid lines evaluate the final model (last iterate); dashed lines evaluate the model obtained by averaging parameters over training (uniform average). Forward rounding causes more error for last iterate, while backward causes more error for the average. (b) Using three bits in the first half of training and one bit in the second, or the reverse, with nearly equal average precision. Each bar divides the SR-induced risk with higher precision early by that with higher precision late. Values above one indicate higher precision at late phase of training outperforms the case with higher precision at early phase of training. (c) Each point selects the smallest tested precision that keeps the final prediction risk no more than 1 % 1\% higher than its value without rounding, at the same width and duration. Both locations use the same precision from 1 to 4 bits. Appendix F gives experimental details.

sections.heading: Summary of main contributions.
sections.text: • Neural scaling laws and compute scaling laws (Section 3 ). We prove general neural scaling laws, showing how prediction error changes with model size, training time and SR precision. For fixed precisions and constant learning rates with parameter averaging, we also derive how the smallest prediction error decreases with compute and which model sizes and training times achieve this scaling under our compute model. • Where, when and how much to round (Sections 4.1 – 4.3 ). Using our scaling laws, we explain which computations need higher precision, when SR is useful during training, and how many needed bits meet an accuracy target. Figure 1 illustrates how the answers change with different predictors, model size and training time. • Learning-rate design and compute allocation (Sections 4.4 – 4.5 ). Our scaling law covers general learning-rate and precision schedules. We show how backward rounding changes learning-rate schedule design and compare precision choices at a fixed compute budget. With a fixed compute budget, lower precision can improve prediction when the benefit of a larger model or longer training outweighs the added rounding error; Figure 3 illustrates this trade-off. For more related work, see Appendix A . Appendices B – E give the mathematical foundations and proofs of our theorems. Appendix F shows the experimental details.

sections.heading: 3 Scaling laws for stochastic-rounding SGD
sections.text: In this section, we give a neural scaling law of the prediction risks in ( 10 ) for general learning-rate and precision schedules, then evaluate it at constant learning rate. The law is decomposed into the error of exact-arithmetic training and the additional error due to rounding. It applies to both outputs in ( 8 ). The difference of their scaling laws explain why they need different precision policies.

sections.heading: How rounding changes the learning curve.
sections.text: For growing width M M and optimization time τ \tau , prediction risk ℛ avg ​ ( T ) \mathscr{R}^{\rm avg}(T) can approach zero even when SR makes it decrease more slowly than its exact-arithmetic counterpart. At fixed positive ρ , σ 2 \rho,\sigma^{2} , with τ → ∞ \tau\to\infty and τ ≤ M a \tau\leq M^{a} from ( 16 ), the exact-arithmetic risk decays as ℛ 0 avg ( T ) ≍ τ − ( b − 1 ) / a \mathscr{R}_{0}^{\rm avg}(T)\asymp\tau^{-(b-1)/a} . The last iterate instead retains an SGD-noise floor of order ρ ​ σ 2 \rho\sigma^{2} , so increasing width and training time alone cannot make its risk vanish at fixed ρ \rho . For the average iterate, preserving the exact-arithmetic risk order requires Δ avg ​ ( T ) = O ⁡ ( ℛ 0 avg ​ ( T ) ) \Delta^{\rm avg}(T)=O(\mathscr{R}_{0}^{\rm avg}(T)) ; rounding error becomes negligible when Δ avg ​ ( T ) = o ⁡ ( ℛ 0 avg ​ ( T ) ) \Delta^{\rm avg}(T)=o(\mathscr{R}_{0}^{\rm avg}(T)) . With forward arithmetic exact and fixed finite backward precision, one can easily check τ = o ⁡ ( M a ) \tau=o(M^{a}) implies ( 21 ) vanishing, whereas preserving the order of ℛ 0 avg ​ ( T ) \mathscr{R}_{0}^{\rm avg}(T) requires τ = O ⁡ ( M a / b ) \tau=O(M^{a/b}) . Thus SR-induced excess risk in ( 21 ) can determine the decay rate even while ℛ avg ​ ( T ) = o ​ ( 1 ) \mathscr{R}^{\rm avg}(T)=o(1) . On the other hand, with SR for both forward and backward passes, τ ≍ M \tau\asymp M with a sufficiently small proportionality constant satisfies ( 22 ) which directly implies that the risk ℛ avg ​ ( T ) \mathscr{R}^{\rm avg}(T) vanishes and rounding error is negligible. Along this family, risk of the uniformly averaged predictor tends to zero as width and training time increase, while both mantissa precisions remain fixed.

sections.heading: 3.3 Compute-optimal scaling law with precision
sections.text: We now use the constant-learning-rate laws to determine how model width and training duration should grow with a compute budget. We focus on the uniformly averaged predictor. We charge the forward and gradient feature computations against a compute budget F F : f := B ​ M ​ ∑ u < T [ c ⁡ ( p fw , u ) + c ⁡ ( p bw , u ) ] ≤ F , c ⁡ ( p ) = { ( p + p 0 ) / ( p ref + p 0 ) , p < ∞ , 1 , p = ∞ . f:=BM\sum_{u<T}[c(p_{\mathrm{fw},u})+c(p_{\mathrm{bw},u})]\leq F,\qquad c(p)=\begin{cases}(p+p_{0})/(p_{\rm ref}+p_{0}),&p<\infty,\\ 1,&p=\infty.\end{cases} (23) Here sign/exponent uses p 0 > 0 p_{0}>0 bits and p ref p_{\rm ref} is a fixed large mantissa bit count for normalization. Each forward or gradient feature computation at precision p p costs B ​ M ​ c ​ ( p ) BM\,c(p) , so fewer bits lower the charge for the same updates. Empirical scaling studies also include precision-dependent training costs ( Kumar et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) . We use the above ( 23 ) to model the compute cost of SGD training in ( 5 ) with different precisions for simplicity. Consider the setup of Section 3.2 with constant η , B \eta,B and fixed precision pair ( p fw , p bw ) (p_{\mathrm{fw}},p_{\mathrm{bw}}) , independently of the budget F F . At each budget, we choose width M M and training duration T T to minimize the prediction risk ℛ avg ​ ( T ) \mathscr{R}^{\rm avg}(T) , subject to f ≤ F f\leq F and the assumptions of Theorem 1 . Table 1 presents compute-optimal scaling laws (the order of the smallest achievable risk), and the orders of M M and τ = η ​ T \tau=\eta T attaining it. The formal statements and proofs are given in Proposition D.5 . Besides, Proposition D.6 justifies the same scaling laws but allowing η , B \eta,B to vary across budgets. Proposition D.7 addresses similar laws for the last iterate predictor. For v T avg v_{T}^{\rm avg} , fixed finite forward precision preserves the exact-arithmetic exponent when backward features remain exact with τ ≍ M a \tau\asymp M^{a} . However, the attaining allocation for backward rounding only uses τ ≍ M a / b \tau\asymp M^{a/b} ; both finite precisions case have τ ≍ M \tau\asymp M . These allocations use progressively more width for a given optimization time, but their risk decays successively more slowly with compute. sections.heading: 4 Implications for low-precision training
sections.text: In this section, we apply scaling laws in Section 3 to answer three precision questions: where rounding is least harmful, when training needs higher precision, and how many bits meet an accuracy target. We then specifically consider learning-rate design and compute allocation. Appendix E gives the full statements and proofs of the claims in this section.

sections.heading: 4.1 Where: rounding location for different predictors
sections.text: Which location in training updates ( 5 ) needs more precision? We compare two different SGD dynamics with different rounding locations: forward-only and backward-only SR in ( 4 ) using the same mantissa bit p p . Let q = 4 − p > 0 q=4^{-p}>0 . For out ∈ { last , avg } {\rm out}\in\{{\rm last},{\rm avg}\} , let Δ out ​ ( q , 0 ) \Delta^{{\rm out}}(q,0) and Δ out ​ ( 0 , q ) \Delta^{{\rm out}}(0,q) denote Δ out ​ ( T ) \Delta^{{\rm out}}(T) in ( 20 ) and ( 21 ) with ( q fw , q bw ) = ( q , 0 ) (q_{\mathrm{fw}},q_{\mathrm{bw}})=(q,0) and ( q fw , q bw ) = ( 0 , q ) (q_{\mathrm{fw}},q_{\mathrm{bw}})=(0,q) , respectively; the other location is exact at each step. Consider τ ≍ M a \tau\asymp M^{a} and setup of Section 3.2 . Proposition E.1 derives the following ratios for SR-induced risk increase: Δ last ​ ( q , 0 ) Δ last ​ ( 0 , q ) ≍ M a − b σ 2 + M 1 − b , Δ avg ​ ( q , 0 ) Δ avg ​ ( 0 , q ) ≍ M 1 − b σ 2 + M 1 − b . \frac{\Delta^{\rm last}(q,0)}{\Delta^{\rm last}(0,q)}\asymp\frac{M^{a-b}}{\sigma^{2}+M^{1-b}},\qquad\frac{\Delta^{\rm avg}(q,0)}{\Delta^{\rm avg}(0,q)}\asymp\frac{M^{1-b}}{\sigma^{2}+M^{1-b}}. (24) With fixed label noise, the first ratio grows as M a − b M^{a-b} and the second decreases as M 1 − b M^{1-b} . Thus, forward-only rounding causes a larger SR-induced error for the last iterate, whereas backward-only rounding leads to a larger error for the uniform average output, for sufficiently large M M . From ( 20 ) to ( 21 ) with τ ≍ M a \tau\asymp M^{a} , averaging makes the forward-only SR-induced error smaller by a factor of order M a − 1 M^{a-1} , whereas backward-only errors have the same order for both outputs. Averaging also reduces exact-arithmetic risk in ( 19 ), so backward rounding error becomes relatively dominant. Figure 1 (a) illustrates this reversal with one-bit rounding at one location. The practical lesson is to choose between the last iterate and the uniform average outputs before allocating precision across computations; under the conditions above, we need higher forward precision for the last iterate and higher backward precision for the uniform average. As a remark, ( 24 ) is only for single precision location comparison, hence when both locations are rounded, the interaction terms related to q fw ​ q bw q_{\mathrm{fw}}q_{\mathrm{bw}} change the overall error behavior. Figure 2 (a) illustrates joint allocation at a fixed total bit count: the best tested split is ( p fw , p bw ) = ( 4 , 1 ) (p_{\mathrm{fw}},p_{\mathrm{bw}})=(4,1) for the last iterate and ( 2 , 3 ) (2,3) for the uniform average.

Proposition E.3 finds the minimizer of N ^ out \widehat{N}^{{\rm out}} as p r , u = { max ⁡ { 0 , log 4 ⁡ ( A r , u / λ ) } , A r , u > 0 , 0 , A r , u = 0 . p_{r,u}=\begin{cases}\max\{0,\log_{4}(A_{r,u}/\lambda)\},&A_{r,u}>0,\\ 0,&A_{r,u}=0.\end{cases} (26) Here λ > 0 \lambda>0 is a constant so that ∑ u < T p r , u = P \sum_{u<T}p_{r,u}=P . sections.heading: 4.5 Model width, training duration, and precision at fixed compute
sections.text: Given compute budget F F in ( 23 ), how should model width, training duration, and precision be chosen, and when can lower precision even improve prediction risk? We now use the uniformly averaged iterate with fixed learning rate η \eta , batch B B and label noise σ 2 \sigma^{2} . We consider the setting of Section 3.2 , accuracy tolerance ϑ \vartheta in ( 27 ) and compute budget F F in ( 23 ).

sections.heading: Fixed precisions: balancing width and training duration.
sections.text: For fixed precisions p fw , p bw p_{\mathrm{fw}},p_{\mathrm{bw}} over training, the compute budget in ( 23 ) bounds M ​ τ M\tau , so increasing width shortens the affordable training duration. In ( 19 ), larger width reduces approximation error, while longer training reduces optimization error. Lower precision reduces compute cost, allowing a wider model and longer training. These additional training steps and larger model reduce approximation and optimization error in ( 19 ). But they improve full prediction risk only when those gains exceed the additional SR-induced error Δ avg ​ ( T ) \Delta^{\rm avg}(T) . Specifically, ( 233 ) in Appendix E gives sufficient conditions on M , τ M,\tau to ensure the accuracy tolerance in ( 27 ). In practice, this means we should choose width M M and training duration T T jointly like the result in Table 1 . Lower precisions can provide more choices of model sizes and training time given a fixed compute budget.

sections.heading: Growing precisions: maintaining accuracy as width increases.
sections.text: How should precision change when model width and training duration increase? The O ⁡ ( 1 ) O(1) terms only depend on the σ \sigma , η \eta , ϑ \vartheta and constants. Backward precision must grow at least logarithmically. Forward precision can remain fixed if backward precision grows enough to meet the total-bit condition. Total mantissa length of order log ⁡ M \log M implies compute f ≍ M a + 1 ​ log ⁡ M f\asymp M^{a+1}\log M which improves the decay exponent in the last row of Table 1 by ℛ avg ( T ) ≍ ( F / log F ) − ( b − 1 ) / ( a + 1 ) . \mathscr{R}^{\rm avg}(T)\asymp(F/\log F)^{-(b-1)/(a+1)}. (32) This scaling only has an additional polylog ⁡ ( F ) \rm{polylog}(F) factor comparing with optimal order F − ( b − 1 ) / ( a + 1 ) F^{-(b-1)/(a+1)} from exact SGD training. Proposition E.8 proves ( 32 ). Hence, increasing precisions logarithmically as model size increases can prevent SR from becoming the accuracy bottleneck as training scales. sections.heading: When does lower precision improve risk at a fixed budget?
sections.text: For fixed width, time, and learning rate, SR cannot reduce the expected risk of the uniformly averaged iterate. Its benefit requires cheaper updates to permit a better training configuration. Compare lower-cost ( L L ) and higher-cost ( H H ) precision choices and fix other training setup the same. Let T L , T H T_{L},T_{H} be time horizons satisfying the same budget in ( 23 ), and Δ L , Δ H \Delta_{L},\Delta_{H} their averaged SR-induced risk increases Δ avg ​ ( T ) \Delta^{\rm avg}(T) . Then the lower precision choice has smaller risk if and only if Δ L − Δ H < ℛ 0 avg ​ ( T H ) − ℛ 0 avg ​ ( T L ) . \Delta_{L}-\Delta_{H}<\mathscr{R}_{0}^{\rm avg}(T_{H})-\mathscr{R}_{0}^{\rm avg}(T_{L}). (33) Appendix E.5.2 presents an example in which ( 33 ) holds. This indicates that lower precision training can outperform exact-arithmetic training at a fixed compute budget by training longer or with a wider model. At fixed width and training duration, lower precision adds rounding error without using the computation it saves. At a fixed compute budget, those savings can instead pay for more training updates or a wider model. Lower precision can therefore reduce total prediction risk when the benefit of the additional training or model capacity exceeds the rounding error.

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: In this section, we examine the compute tradeoffs in Section 4.5 , then study data reuse and neural-network computations beyond our theoretical analysis. Consider a = 2 a=2 , b = 3 / 2 b=3/2 , σ 2 = 0.1 \sigma^{2}=0.1 , B = 32 B=32 and d = 4 ​ M d=4M . In simulations we may train beyond τ T = M a \tau_{T}=M^{a} , so these comparisons do not follow all assumptions of Theorem 1 . Compute follows ( 23 ). Appendix F shows the experimental details.

sections.heading: Width and training duration at fixed compute.
sections.text: Figure 3 illustrates the joint choice of width, duration and precision in Section 4.5 for uniformly averaged outputs. Figure 3 (a,b) compare prediction risks across widths. Both red dashed curves use the exact-arithmetic scaling F − 1 / 6 F^{-1/6} in Table 1 . Figure 3 (b) has better optimal scaling than the joint-SR scaling F − 1 / 8 F^{-1/8} in Table 1 , since simulation here does not impose all conditions of Theorem 1 . In Figure 3 (c), joint one-bit SR permits a wider model and longer training, reducing mean prediction risk by 9.7 % 9.7\% at the same compute budget among the tested configurations. The gain from a wider model and longer training outweighs the SR-induced error: precision should be selected together with width and time by comparing full risks at a fixed compute budget.

sections.heading: Data reuse at fixed compute.
sections.text: Figure 4 asks whether SR updates remain useful when training revisits existing examples during training. At fixed width and compute cap F = 2 27 F=2^{27} , with fresh data or either reused dataset, lower precision allows longer training and wider model. The uniform average output then achieves about 5% lower prediction risk than exact-arithmetic training. Figure 4 (b) shows lower mean prediction risk for low-precision training at every tested compute budget. Additional training offsets the SR-induced error, as in ( 33 ). The more data reused, the lower the prediction risk in Figure 4 (c). Thus the compute benefit can persist with data reuse. We leave a data-reuse scaling law with SR for future work. sections.heading: Precision choices in neural networks.
sections.text: Figure 5 extends the location question in Section 4.1 to a six-layer transformer trained on 200M FineWeb-Edu tokens and a CIFAR-10 MLP. The combined rounding configuration has higher transformer validation loss than activation-only rounding in Figure 5 (a). Our theory only considered independent rounding of features in ( 4 ). Sharing introduces dependence between rounding errors. Figure 5 (b) compares this independent rounding with shared rounding, which reuses the same rounded activation for the forward computation and the weight-gradient computation. Remarkably, it shows that sharing the rounded activation between forward and weight-gradient computations also changes performance. At one bit, sharing lowers the validation losses relative to independent rounding for both models. Compared with training without SR, shared rounding gives lower loss for MLP but higher loss for transformer. Figure 5 (c) separates rounding during training from rounding at test time. The one-bit forward-trained MLP has test loss 1.624 1.624 without SR during test-time predictions and 1.672 1.672 with forward-activation SR at test time. Precision comparisons should therefore specify all rounded computations and whether activations are shared, and compare models with SR disabled at test time before assessing low-precision inference. Figure 5: Rounding locations, shared activations and test-time prediction in neural networks. (a) Final transformer validation loss; the combined case rounds both activation computations, incoming gradients and forward weights to two bits, with seven-bit parameter storage. (b) Shared SR reuses the same forward-rounded activation in the weight-gradient computation. Points show final loss differences from same-seed training with SR and without SR. Negative values indicate lower loss than this baseline. (c) Each trained MLP is tested twice with its parameters fixed: with forward-activation SR disabled, and with SR enabled at its training precision. Both tests use the same examples. Appendix F.5 gives details and final performance values.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We derived scaling laws for stochastic rounding in random-feature regression. Precision, model size and training time should be chosen together. Under our compute model, lower precision can improve prediction at a fixed budget when the benefits of a larger model or longer training outweigh the added rounding error. The learning rates and the choice to average model parameters also affect where and when higher precision is needed. Extending the theory to data reuse, more quantization locations, feature learning regimes ( Ba et al., 2022 ) , and measuring savings on hardware, remain future work.

sections.heading: Appendix A Related work
sections.text: This appendix reviews work on scaling laws, quantization and stochastic rounding, and explains how our model and results relate to these studies.

sections.heading: Empirical scaling laws.
sections.text: Scaling laws try to analyze how loss changes as model size, sample size and compute increasing ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) , with extensions to continual weather training ( Subramanian et al., 2026 ) . Kumar et al. (2025) ; Sun et al. (2025) use fitted laws to choose model size, the number of data points and precision for a given compute budget. Related work studies scaling in quantization-aware training ( Chen et al., 2026a ) and joint quantization and sparsity ( Frantar et al., 2025 ) . Kim et al. (2026) extend fitted laws to different forward and backward precisions and hardware-dependent compute costs.

sections.heading: Theory of scaling law.
sections.text: One of the solvable models for scaling law is the random feature model ( Mei and Montanari, 2022 ; Bach, 2024 ; LeJeune et al., 2024 ; Cheng and Montanari, 2024 ; Defilippis et al., 2024 ) . Linear models with power-law random features (PLRF) have been applied to theoretically understand the scaling law of prediction risk ( Bahri et al., 2024 ; Maloney et al., 2022 ; Bordelon et al., 2024 ; Bordelon and Pehlevan, 2022 ; Paquette et al., 2024 ; Paquette et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2024 ) . These results are also extended to the setting of data-reuse SGD ( Lin et al., 2025 ) , mini-batch control ( Chen et al., 2026b ) and general learning-rate schedules ( Bordelon and Mori, 2026 ) . Power-law spectra have also been observed and analyzed in trained weights of networks ( Hodgkinson et al., 2025 ; Martin and Mahoney, 2019 ; Martin and Mahoney, 2020 ; Martin et al., 2021 ) .

sections.heading: Quantization in linear regression.
sections.text: Zhang et al. (2026a) derive prediction-risk upper bounds for linear regression with quantized data, labels, parameters, activations and gradients. Zhang et al. (2026b) study scaling laws with model size and training data in sketched linear regression, giving upper and lower bounds for their quantization models. Both use constant learning rates and parameter averaging. Their general upper bounds allow unbiased quantization, while their scaling results make additional assumptions on rounding-error covariance. Our quantization from SR does not generally follow their multiplicative or additive quantization assumptions. Our laws also cover last-iterate predictor, and general learning-rate and precision schedules.

sections.heading: Low-precision training.
sections.text: QAT uses low-precision weights and activations during training for efficient inference ( Jacob et al., 2018 ; Esser et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . Low-precision training methods include BinaryConnect ( Courbariaux et al., 2015 ) , quantized gradients ( Zhou et al., 2016 ) , SR training ( Gupta et al., 2015 ) , and direct low-precision weight updates ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) . Theoretical works can be found by Li et al. (2017) ; De Sa et al. (2018) . Practical LLMs use FP8, MXFP4, and FP4 in training ( Micikevicius et al., 2022 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2024 ; Tseng et al., 2025 ; Castro et al., 2025 ; Chmiel et al., 2025 ; Panferov et al., 2026 ) . Zhang et al. (2017) use independent rounding in ( 4 ) for low-precision training. Learned precision ( Yu et al., 2022 ) and learning-rate schedules ( Wolfe and Kyrillidis, 2024 ) for low-precision training studied how precision and optimization choices work together.

sections.heading: Numerical analysis for SR.
sections.text: Higham and Mary (2019) ; Higham and Mary (2020) ; Connolly et al. (2021) ; El Arar et al. (2023) ; Croci et al. (2022) analyze the bound of the rounding error for SR in numerical computations. Other work also studies SR with few random bits ( Fitzgibbon and Felix, 2025 ) , computational complexity ( Drineas and Ipsen, 2024 ) , and its effects on small singular values of random matrices ( Boutsikas et al., 2024 ; Dexter et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . We refer to El Arar et al. (2026) as a comprehensive review of SR theory, hardware and applications.

sections.heading: Appendix B Stochastic rounding and sketch geometry
sections.text: This appendix develops the rounding identities and random-feature geometry used to prove Theorem 1 in Appendix D.1 . Lemmas B.1 – B.2 bound Gaussian rounding moments, and Proposition B.3 derives the training second-moment recursions. Proposition B.9 combines the spectral, teacher and rounding-coordinate bounds into one high-probability sketch event used in the subsequent analysis.

sections.heading: B.1 Shared notation and second-moment comparison
sections.text: We define the oracle predictor and second moments used in the training recursions of Proposition B.3 . Throughout this appendix, unless a sketch probability is stated, expectations condition on S S and average over the teacher, training data and rounding variables.

sections.heading: Appendix C General learning-rate and precision schedules
sections.text: This appendix bounds the second moments that determine prediction risk for general learning-rate and precision schedules. Theorem C.3 gives risk identities and exact-arithmetic moment bounds, and Lemma C.4 controls the additional state moments caused by rounding. Theorem C.6 and Proposition C.7 give matching bounds for the SR-induced output risk, which Appendix D.1 converts into Theorem 1 . Appendix C.6 constructs the admissibility thresholds used throughout. In this appendix, condition on a sketch S S in the event of Proposition B.9 . Write Θ = C θ tr \Theta=C_{\theta}^{\rm tr} and τ ∗ = τ ∗ sch \tau_{*}=\tau_{*}^{\rm sch} . The symbols c , C c,C denote positive constants depending only on the fixed model, the comparison tuple of Definition B.8 , c 0 c_{0} , the minimum cumulative learning rate τ ∗ \tau_{*} and the positive noise variance. They do not depend on width, horizon, batch size or the learning-rate and precision schedules. Their construction is given in Appendix C.6 .

sections.text: This appendix derives the design consequences discussed in Section 4 . Proposition E.1 compares rounding locations and outputs; Propositions E.2 – E.4 address precision allocation across training; and Corollary E.5 gives bit requirements for a prescribed risk tolerance. Only the last iterate and uniform average are considered with Assumption C.1 . Use the constant-schedule notation of Section 3.2 . Corollary B.5 justifies replacing sketch-dependent noise by its deterministic scale, including when the bias term is added.

sections.heading: F.5 Neural-network rounding locations and evaluation
sections.text: Figure 5 reports final transformer validation loss and MLP test loss, both cross-entropy using natural logarithms. Training without SR disables only the added experimental stochastic-rounding operations. Evaluation means making predictions and calculating validation or test loss after training, with parameters fixed and no further updates. It disables the added SR operations unless stated otherwise; the underlying arithmetic described below remains unchanged. Bit counts refer to mantissa precision, with unrestricted exponents.

sections.heading: Models and training.
sections.text: The transformer has six layers, six heads, width 384, context 256 and 30,041,856 parameters. It trains on approximately 200 million FineWeb-Edu tokens for 12,207 updates, with batches of 64 × 256 64\times 256 tokens. AdamW uses peak learning rate 6 × 10 − 4 6\times 10^{-4} , coefficients ( 0.9 , 0.95 ) (0.9,0.95) , weight decay 0.1 0.1 , gradient clipping at one and 100 warmup updates. We use three seeds and 40 fixed validation batches. All transformer runs use BF16/FP32 mixed-precision arithmetic, with BF16 autocast enabled during both training and evaluation, including when added SR is disabled. The CIFAR-10 MLP has architecture 3072 3072 – 1024 1024 – 10 10 with ReLU and FP32 computation. It trains for 25 epochs (9750 updates), batch size 128, using SGD with momentum 0.9 0.9 , weight decay 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} , peak learning rate 0.01 0.01 and 200 warmup updates. We use 16 seeds and the full CIFAR-10 test set. Both models decrease the learning rate linearly during the final 20 % 20\% of training and report last-iterate performance.

Scaling Laws for SGD with Stochastic Rounding Zhichao Wang ICSI and Department of Statistics University of California, Berkeley, USA zhichao.wang@berkeley.edu Michael W. Mahoney ICSI, LBNL and Department of Statistics University of California, Berkeley, USA mmahoney@stat.berkeley.edu Abstract Low-precision training reduces computation but introduces additional rounding error. We study how stochastic rounding (SR) affects prediction risk as model size, training time and precision change. We consider a two-layer linear network with a fixed random first layer, trained by mini-batch SGD on fresh Gaussian data with power-law spectra. At each SGD step, the features used in forward and backward computations are rounded independently. We prove matched upper and lower bounds on prediction error for the final model and for uniform parameter averaging, with general learning-rate and precision schedules chosen before training. For fixed precisions and constant learning rates with parameter averaging, we derive how the smallest prediction error decreases with compute and identify model sizes and training times that achieve this optimal-compute scaling. Rounding only the forward features preserves the compute scaling of exact arithmetic, while rounding backward features changes it. Averaging parameters can change which computation needs higher precision and when higher precision is useful. The laws also give bit requirements for a given accuracy tolerance and show how backward rounding changes learning-rate schedule design. At a fixed compute budget, lower precision can improve prediction when the benefit of a larger model or longer training outweighs the additional SR-induced error. Model simulations illustrate these tradeoffs, and experiments with an MLP and a small transformer examine rounding choices beyond the theoretical model. 1 Introduction Training large machine learning models in low precision can reduce memory usage and computational costs. For example, mixed-precision training computes matrix multiplications of the forward and backward passes in 16-bit arithmetic while keeping a high-precision copy of the weights ( Micikevicius et al., 2018 ) . Recent LLMs are even pretrained with 8-bit and 4-bit floating-point matrix products ( Micikevicius et al., 2022 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2024 ; Tseng et al., 2025 ; Castro et al., 2025 ; Chmiel et al., 2025 ; Panferov et al., 2026 ) . Meanwhile, quantization-aware training (QAT) simulates low-precision weights and activations during training, making the trained model run in low precision at inference ( Jacob et al., 2018 ; Esser et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . A third setting saves training memory by quantizing the activations saved for backpropagation, while leaving the forward pass unchanged ( Chen et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) . Separately, Chen et al. (2020) show extra gradient variance caused by rounding in fully quantized training, where weights, activations and gradients are quantized. In this paper, we focus on the first setting, in which the arithmetic of training itself is rounded. Stochastic rounding (SR) rounds a number to one of its neighboring representable values with probabilities that preserve the input value in expectation. This unbiasedness can avoid update stagnation at precisions where round-to-nearest stalls ( Gupta et al., 2015 ; Zhang et al., 2017 ; De Sa et al., 2018 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Ozkara et al., 2025 ) . Existing SR theory provides probabilistic bounds on rounding errors in numerical computations ( Higham and Mary, 2019 ; Higham and Mary, 2020 ; Connolly et al., 2021 ; Croci et al., 2022 ; El Arar et al., 2023 ; Drineas and Ipsen, 2024 ; El Arar et al., 2026 ) and convergence guarantees for low-precision SGD ( Li et al., 2017 ; De Sa et al., 2018 ; Ozkara et al., 2025 ) . Its benefit on small singular values has also been studied ( Boutsikas et al., 2024 ; Dexter et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . These results do not further describe how prediction risk depends jointly on model width, training time and precision, or how to allocate precision bits across operations and training steps. So we aim to answer the following question in this paper: Where, when, and with how many bits should we use stochastic rounding during training? To answer this question, we prove a neural scaling law, which describes how loss asymptotically decreases with model size, training time and compute ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ; Subramanian et al., 2026 ) , This law practically guides the allocation of compute resources during training. Recent empirical work extends these laws to low-precision training and model quantization ( Kumar et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Frantar et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . Typically, Kumar et al. (2025) ; Sun et al. (2025) empirically use fitted scaling laws to choose model size, training data and precision for a given compute budget. These findings motivate a theoretical study of precision-dependent loss scaling and quantitative analyses of training dynamics with quantization ( Zhang et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . In the exact-arithmetic setting, theory of neural scaling law has been extensively studied ( Bahri et al., 2024 ; Maloney et al., 2022 ; Bordelon et al., 2024 ; Paquette et al., 2024 ; Paquette et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2025 ; Bordelon and Mori, 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) . Specifically, Paquette et al. (2024) gives the baseline compute optimal scaling law. We follow these results and study a two-layer linear network with a fixed random first layer and train its output layer using online SGD with SR. We consider both the final model and a model formed by averaging parameters during training. And the features used in the forward and backward computations are rounded independently, possibly at different precisions over the training. Kim et al. (2026) concurrently fit separate forward/backward precision effects and hardware-aware allocations, supported by a convex-optimization upper bound. We theoretically derive binary-SR risk scaling laws and optimal compute allocations in low precision. Figure 1: (a) We round the features either at forward pass or backward pass in SGD dynamics ( 5 ) with one-bit precision and compare the SR-induced error over the corresponding risk without rounding. Solid lines evaluate the final model (last iterate); dashed lines evaluate the model obtained by averaging parameters over training (uniform average). Forward rounding causes more error for last iterate, while backward causes more error for the average. (b) Using three bits in the first half of training and one bit in the second, or the reverse, with nearly equal average precision. Each bar divides the SR-induced risk with higher precision early by that with higher precision late. Values above one indicate higher precision at late phase of training outperforms the case with higher precision at early phase of training. (c) Each point selects the smallest tested precision that keeps the final prediction risk no more than 1 % 1\% higher than its value without rounding, at the same width and duration. Both locations use the same precision from 1 to 4 bits. Appendix F gives experimental details. Summary of main contributions. • Neural scaling laws and compute scaling laws (Section 3 ). We prove general neural scaling laws, showing how prediction error changes with model size, training time and SR precision. For fixed precisions and constant learning rates with parameter averaging, we also derive how the smallest prediction error decreases with compute and which model sizes and training times achieve this scaling under our compute model. • Where, when and how much to round (Sections 4.1 – 4.3 ). Using our scaling laws, we explain which computations need higher precision, when SR is useful during training, and how many needed bits meet an accuracy target. Figure 1 illustrates how the answers change with different predictors, model size and training time. • Learning-rate design and compute allocation (Sections 4.4 – 4.5 ). Our scaling law covers general learning-rate and precision schedules. We show how backward rounding changes learning-rate schedule design and compare precision choices at a fixed compute budget. With a fixed compute budget, lower precision can improve prediction when the benefit of a larger model or longer training outweighs the added rounding error; Figure 3 illustrates this trade-off. For more related work, see Appendix A . Appendices B – E give the mathematical foundations and proofs of our theorems.
